docs/competition/competition-boards.md:9:Competition uses a subset of the sizes already supported by the solo game. Quarterfinals are played on 4x4, semifinals on 6x6 and finals on 8x8. There is no new board geometry involved: each is an existing square grid handled by the current deck and board components.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:35:All face numbers used by the boards in this page are below 64, so they use the solid variant. The smallest board contains the eight shapes with the top marker. The middle board includes additional marker directions, and the largest reaches through four marker groups. This gives reviewers a more precise explanation of increasing visual complexity than saying only that there are more cards.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:37:For instance, the circle shape can appear with different marker directions on a larger board. Recognizing a familiar outline of a shape is therefore less informative than recognizing the full face. The player-facing introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker for this reason. The deck still compares face numbers; it does not award a partial match for two similar shapes.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:55:This is an easy source of misleading manual notes. A researcher can write down “card 17” while watching one board and later open a different size. Without the board context, the note no longer identifies the same visible location. Board codes carry the side length; a loose position number does not.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:63:How that context is presented during a group session remains a separate design subject. The board dimensions for the stages use the existing size support in the source.
docs/competition/competition-boards.md:65:One useful comparison in a visual review is the same board early and late in play, at the same viewport width. That isolates the change in exposed artwork from the change in grid dimensions. A second comparison across the three dimensions then makes the actual growth visible. The two comparisons answer different questions and avoid attributing every difficulty on a larger board to its card count alone.

1:# Persistence envelope
3:This page describes the feature storage envelope and distinguishes it from the preference format already implemented in Neon Pairs.
5:The source currently serializes a preference aggregate, not a collection of feature records. Its key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and its discriminator is `schemaVersion: 1`. The existing reader and writer continue to use that preference format; values already stored in browsers require a code migration to change shape.
9:A feature's stored collection has an outer representation and a collection of domain records inside it. The envelope carries the format identity at that outer boundary, before any individual record can be interpreted. Every value a feature adds to browser storage is a JSON object with exactly two keys: "v", the number 3, and "items", the array of records. The records carry the feature's data, while the outer object identifies the representation used to hold that collection.
11:This makes a feature value inspectable without relying on the name of a variable in the UI. A reader can distinguish an outer format mismatch from a problem in a particular record. The envelope is separate from the record schema, storage key, ordering field and identity scheme. The current preferences implementation stores a selected size and a best-score map rather than feature records.
13:The envelope also does not change board-code, snapshot or replay formats. Those are interchange representations with their own version identifiers and validation. A snapshot copied by the player is not a preference save, and a replay read by the developer command is not a browser collection. See [Format versioning guide](../sharing/format-versioning-guide.md) and [Data exchange policy](../sharing/data-exchange-policy.md) when following a value across those boundaries.
17:The current storage writer does this:
29:This object remembers a selected 8x8 size, a 4x4 best of 8 moves and an 8x8 best of 40. The score map is keyed by board size rather than represented as a sequence of attempts. It has no recency information. Its version number is not inferred from the suffix on the storage key: the reader checks the numeric discriminator inside the value as well.
31:There is no feature-envelope serializer or decoder in `src/game/session/storage.ts`. `readPreferences` expects the existing aggregate, and feeding it a feature-shaped collection returns the default preference state. Conversely, no current browser code loads feature records and turns them into the preference map. The two representations have different jobs and are not interchangeable encodings of the same object.
37:`readPreferences` starts with `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` as its fallback. It obtains the stored string, passes it through `parseJson`, requires a non-null non-array object, checks the version and selected size, and then checks the score map. A single rejected map entry returns the fallback for the whole preference value.
43:The feature envelope's boundary should not be inferred from that lenience. Its stated outer shape is its own contract. A convenience helper existing nearby does not decide which parser uses it or what a particular version accepts.
47:The project has a product specification version, a preference schema version and explicit interchange format versions. They are not one counter. The current specification identifies itself as 2.2 while the preference discriminator remains 1. A feature envelope uses the numeric version described in its own boundary. A board code's prefix describes its generation algorithm rather than the layout of browser preference JSON.
49:Keeping those meanings distinct avoids a common support mistake: assuming a newer app release must reject every older saved object. The preferences are accepted according to `PREFERENCES_VERSION` and field validation. The product release number is not read from storage, compared to storage or written into the preference object.
51:There is no migration chain in the preference store. An unsupported discriminator produces the same fallback as a malformed value. No code attempts to guess an older shape, rename its fields or convert a saved sequence into a best map. A migration requires a code change with observable effects.
55:It helps to follow one ordinary preference update from the UI rather than treating storage as a single operation. Selecting a different grid size creates a new game. `replaceGame` copies the session preferences and changes `size` to the new board's side length. React renders using that state. The save effect then calls `writePreferences`, which constructs the versioned object, serializes it and passes the string to the supplied store.
59:An envelope serves a similar boundary role for its own record collection, but there is no existing generic persistence framework to extend. The source uses direct imports and a two-method store interface. There is no registry, adapter hierarchy or global storage coordinator.
63:An empty preference score map is valid. It means no supported size has a saved best in that aggregate. The selected size is still meaningful. By contrast, an absent score-map field, an array in its place, or a map with an impossible score invalidates the preference value. Missing storage and invalid storage reach the same fallback state through different branches.
67:Empty data should also be distinguished from unavailable storage. A reader can return an empty state after a denied read, but that return value alone does not prove that the browser is ready to accept a future write. In the preferences API, failure information is intentionally not returned to the caller. The feature failure presentation described in [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) consequently cannot be obtained just by inspecting an empty map.
73:For preferences, compare the inner `schemaVersion` with `PREFERENCES_VERSION`, then the selected size with `GRID_SIZES`, then each score key and value with the reader's checks. A key spelled `04` is rejected even though converting it to a number yields 4. A score of 7 for a 4x4 board is rejected because eight pairs require at least eight moves. A value can be syntactically valid JSON while failing either of those semantic checks.
75:For a feature collection, inspect the outer representation before speculating about domain records. A test result for preference JSON is not evidence about feature-record acceptance. Stored values can share a storage mechanism while using different validators.
89:The list representation is discussed in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). Parsing and validation failures are covered in [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md), because retention of accepted records and recovery from rejected input are different operations.
105:This makes the data easy to explain: a valid best remains available across normal reloads until another relevant event changes the storage or the value is rejected. A better result can replace it. Browser policy or a person's site-data action can remove it. Another tab can overwrite the aggregate. None of those is an application age policy.
107:The distinction matters when comparing evidence from two visits. A gap between visits does not by itself identify the cause of a missing best. If the origin changed, the second visit may have read another storage area. If the value was edited into an invalid shape, the reader may have used its fallback. If the browser cleared data, the key may simply be absent. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) discusses environment-driven loss without treating it as list pruning.
115:`rememberBest` returns the original object for equal or worse results. The session can still render a completed game, but the preference identity need not change. This keeps the storage effect aligned with meaningful preference updates in that path. It is not a universal deduplication layer: replacement actions can still write the same serialized preference contents again.
117:For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.
121:The app has no account or service that copies the aggregate elsewhere. A best kept in one profile remains local to that browser's storage context. Opening the same HTML in another browser does not fetch it. Exporting a snapshot copies game progress, not a backup of the browser's accumulated bests or selected-size history.
123:The UI has no general preference export, browser-data restore or clear-records control. A developer can inspect or change storage manually, but those are debugging actions rather than product controls.
127:A bounded collection makes its record count predictable. It does not guarantee every write succeeds: browser access can be blocked before capacity matters, and another application on the same origin may consume storage. A small value can fail to write even though its own size is well below a browser's nominal limit.
129:Conversely, a successful write does not prove indefinite lifetime. The browser can later clear data, a private context can end, or the person can remove site storage. Those environmental conditions are outside the saved-list retention operation. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) describes how a value can survive a reload yet disappear when the browsing session ends.
135:The existing test suite establishes preference behavior rather than a list API. `storage.test.ts` checks independent minimums for two sizes and object identity for equal and worse results. Browser journeys check that completed bests survive reloads and game resets. None of those tests asserts a sequence of saved feature records.
139:It is also useful to keep failed writes separate from successful retention checks. A denied store can leave the feature's in-memory state ahead of the browser value. Inspecting the old browser string then proves only that the write failed, not that the retention calculation chose the wrong records. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) describes the store doubles that make this separation observable.
143:The best map cannot answer how many attempts occurred, which deal produced a best, how long that attempt took, or whether two equal results happened on different days. None of those fields is retained. A new feature that needs a collection has a different persistence concern from calculating a size-specific minimum.
146:# Storage failure policy
148:This page describes how unavailable browser storage affects play and how saved-record features present that limitation.
150:The current game isolates storage failures from the active game. It catches errors while obtaining the browser store, reading the preference key and writing its replacement. The session can hold its selected size and best results in memory even when no durable write succeeds. There is no current preference-storage warning in the rendered game.
154:For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.
156:The preference adapter does not yet expose a blocked-status result. `readPreferences` returns a `Preferences` value in all cases, and `writePreferences` returns `void`. Neither return type carries an availability flag or failure reason. `Game.tsx` renders no preference-storage warning; saved-record features have separate failure feedback.
162:The first operation is acquiring the storage object. `browserStore` in `src/game/session/use-saved-preferences.ts` returns `window.localStorage` inside a `try` block. If the property getter throws, the function catches the exception and returns `null`. A denied property getter is tested in `tests/browser-environment.e2e.test.ts` by defining a getter that throws a `SecurityError` before the game initializes.
168:These stages explain why a single boolean based on the existence of the storage property would be a weak diagnostic. The game doesn't use such a probe. It attempts the real operation at the boundary and catches failure there.
172:Storage failure does not bypass the game's own rules. Card eligibility, move counting, matching, elapsed time and completion still use their normal state transitions. The fallback affects the initial preference value and the durability of subsequent changes. It does not substitute a different deck algorithm or change how many moves a result takes.
176:If storage remains unavailable, a page reload starts another session from the fallback. The earlier in-memory best is gone with the old page. This is the expected consequence of unsuccessful saving, even though play in the earlier page was complete and valid. A report that a score survived Restart but disappeared on reload is consistent with a write failure.
178:An imported unfinished snapshot remains usable under the same conditions. The snapshot text is decoded into game state, then the session handles pause and resume. That path does not require a successful preference write. The accepted board size may be retained only in the current session if the browser refuses the later save.
190:There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.
192:If the captured store object exists and its methods change behavior, a later effect can succeed using the same object. For example, a test double can reject its first write and accept a later one. That is different from reacquiring a previously inaccessible property. Both cases can be modeled without making the game rules aware of browser error names.
194:The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.
202:[Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) follows the rejection branches in detail. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) explains why the small size of this app's own payload cannot establish that a shared origin has available space.
206:The source only calls `getItem` and `setItem` for `PREFERENCES_KEY`. It has no storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. `PreferenceStore` exposes only those two methods. The storage unit test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.
214:`storage.test.ts` uses a denied store whose read and write methods both throw. It checks that reading yields the default size and that writing does not throw. It also covers `readPreferences(null)`. This verifies the API boundary directly, without needing to configure an actual browser's privacy settings.
216:The browser environment test covers a different boundary: acquisition of `window.localStorage`. It installs the throwing getter before loading the game, loads a fixed board and matches a known pair. The harness gathers uncaught page errors and checks that none occurred. That demonstrates continued play after an acquisition failure, not persistence in that denied context.
218:These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.
220:# Dialog policy
222:This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions.
224:The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.
226:## The confirmation boundary
228:A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision.
230:There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved.
236:`Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used.
238:BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation.
240:The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure.
242:This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle.
246:The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board.
250:The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.
252:No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices.
256:A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.
258:Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the established clock model.
260:Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.
266:Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target.
268:After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.
272:The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).
278:A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements.
280:Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.
285:This page records the treatment of person-entered names and distinguishes it from the game's existing code and JSON fields.
287:Neon Pairs currently asks for a board code and snapshot text, not a player name. There is no name field, group-name store or name rendering component in the source. The name policy below applies when such input is introduced; it does not describe a transformation already applied to the reproduction textarea.
289:## One name representation
291:A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another.
293:The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats.
295:For names, the other checks are documented separately in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). This page explains representation and input boundaries without duplicating their conditions or error messages.
299:The following examples use quotes only to make surrounding whitespace visible. The quotes are not part of the entered name.
303:| `  Mira  ` | `Mira` | Space around the name is removed |
309:The last example matters because representation cleanup is not an instruction to remove meaningful punctuation or rewrite a person's preferred spelling. The policy does not transliterate scripts, strip accents or convert names to ASCII. Those would be additional transformations beyond what is stated.
311:NFC addresses canonical equivalence in Unicode text. It is not the compatibility normalization form. Text that merely looks similar is not necessarily canonically equivalent, and this policy does not define visual resemblance as identity. That boundary prevents a representation step from quietly becoming a broad name-matching heuristic.
313:A name can also contain multiple words. Collapsing a whitespace run does not merge words together; it leaves a separating space. Treating the policy as “delete all whitespace” would change `Ada Lovelace` into a different string and would not implement the stated behavior.
317:A draft is what someone is still editing. A stored value is what an action has accepted. The policy determines the representation of accepted and displayed names, but it does not prescribe that the caret jump after every keystroke or that an input method's partial composition be rewritten while it is active.
319:That distinction leaves room to implement an editing experience without confusing it with persistence. A reviewer can inspect where a completed entry crosses from local draft state into the feature's model and where the model is rendered. If display uses an old raw draft while storage uses the processed value, the two surfaces no longer have the relationship described above.
321:The current Reproduction component provides a useful example of draft ownership, though its data is not a name. Its snapshot string lives in local React state and is sent to the decoder on Load snapshot. BoardCodeForm instead reads its native form field at submission. Either storage approach can host an input boundary; the choice of controlled or uncontrolled field does not by itself implement name representation.
323:No name persistence shape exists in `session/storage.ts`. Its preferences concern size and best move counts. Those fields contain no name preference key, snapshot property or import format.
331:Successful submission replaces the game and refreshes the field from the current code because the input is keyed by generation. Unsuccessful submission preserves the draft. This gives a concrete reference for separating a draft from an accepted representation without applying name transformations to a deal identifier. See [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).
339:Applying name cleanup to the entire JSON draft would conflate two kinds of input. Whitespace can occur between tokens or inside a JSON string, with different meanings. The existing code passes the complete draft to `decodeSnapshot`; it does not first treat it as display prose or a person's name.
341:The same is true for error preservation. On malformed JSON, the text remains editable and the current game remains present. That behavior supports correction of a structured draft. Accepted names use the normalized representation described above.
349:The policy also leaves capitalization alone at this representation step. A comparison operation may have its own policy, but that does not require changing a person's displayed capitalization. Keeping display representation and comparison purpose distinct avoids presenting a comparison key as someone's chosen name.
351:Likewise, a font's treatment of a character does not change the text stored. A missing glyph, a ligature or a different script's shaping belongs to rendering and typography. The representation policy can be implemented correctly while a layout still needs work to display the name legibly. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) provides the visual context.
353:The current game has no name-character allowlist or prohibited-name list. Adding one while implementing spacing cleanup would be a separate product decision, not a consequence of Unicode normalization.
357:There are no name-specific tests in the repository because no name entry has been implemented. The useful evidence for a future implementation would connect its draft, accepted model and displayed text using the cases above. A check confined to an input's current value can miss a storage path that retains an older raw string.
359:Repeated processing should not progressively change the accepted spelling. The transformations described here have a stable result once applied. If editing, saving and displaying the same accepted name repeatedly removes more content each time, that points to an implementation doing more than the stated representation work.
361:The current code's strongest relevant lesson is explicit boundaries: BoardCodeForm submits a draft, the controller validates, replacement updates the model, and rendered controls follow that model. Names need their own representation boundary within the feature that introduces them. The present board-code and snapshot controls use their own input boundaries.
362:# Name length policy
364:This page defines how the name-length check is interpreted and separates it from native text-field limits.
366:The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page.
370:The length check concerns the accepted name representation, after the processing described in [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Counting the raw draft instead can produce a different result from counting the value that the feature will store and display. A name has 2 to 20 Unicode code points after normalization. Anything else blocks the action and shows "Use 2 to 20 characters." This check therefore belongs at the point where a draft would become an accepted name, rather than being inferred from the field's apparent width.
372:The message is the user-facing explanation of this failure. The numerical bounds are inclusive: the endpoints pass, and values outside them fail. The policy does not define an exception for a one-character name, a separate limit for a family name or an alternate bound for another script.
374:A failure blocks the action that is trying to accept the name. It is not a request to silently cut the entered value to fit. Truncating a longer string would accept a different name and would conceal which action failed. The policy specifies feedback and blocking rather than a repair that guesses the user's intended spelling.
378:JavaScript string `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. That is not always the number required here. Many characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane occupy two code units but one Unicode code point. For example, `A😀` has three code units and two code points.
384:In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper.
402:“Passes” here means that the length condition is satisfied. It does not imply that an action with other applicable checks is guaranteed to succeed. The [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) addresses a separate group-level condition without changing the unit used by this check.
406:A raw draft may have surrounding or repeated spacing that will not be retained in its accepted form. Counting before the representation step can reject a value that would fit after processing, or accept a value whose later transformations were not what the length helper expected. The policy's ordering avoids having the stored name disagree with the checked name.
408:A reviewer can follow one candidate from field submission to accepted model and then display. The decisive value is the same one used for the count. An implementation that checks one temporary string but saves a different raw draft has two representations and cannot establish the stated condition simply by having a correctly named length function.
414:There is no name-length test in the repository. Keyboard and reproduction checks establish native field labels, draft preservation and load outcomes. They do not verify the name count merely because they type strings into controls.
416:When this policy is implemented, its evidence can name the processed candidate and observed outcome at the boundary. That is enough to distinguish a counting defect from a display problem or another group-level validation failure. The policy stays narrow: one accepted value, one counting unit, one inclusive interval and the stated blocking message.
417:# Duplicate names policy
419:This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it.
421:The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.
425:The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.
427:The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.
429:The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.
433:Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes.
435:A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name.
437:The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies.
443:| Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates |
446:| `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names |
448:| `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text |
451:These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name.
453:A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form.
457:A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated.
461:The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) provides the current feedback mechanics.
465:Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization.
467:Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only repeat, a repeat that is not adjacent in the displayed list and a different accepted name. An edit scenario reveals whether the current entry is being confused with another entry. A separate-group example reveals whether an implementation accidentally enforces a broader scope than the policy states.
490:A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`.
507:A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) follows those two sources in a complete game.
562:# Tables policy
566:There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.
570:When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.
572:This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.
578:GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.
580:The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.
586:## Why the card board is not a table
588:Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.
590:The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.
592:There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.
596:An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.
598:The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.
600:A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.
606:A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.
612:The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.
614:There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.
616:Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) and [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.
618:The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.

2:This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.
8:## Existing formats and new exports
10:The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.
12:There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See [Format versioning](format-versioning-guide.md) for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.
14:Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.
24:| Did a local best survive reload? | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record |
36:A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. [Replay format](replay-format.md) covers the timeline and diagnostic result.
38:None of these objects contains a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Those values have different lifetimes and authorities. A loaded board's size becomes the chosen size through session replacement; that is a browser consequence of loading, not a separate field in the artifact. A completed import is displayed without recording an import as a new played result.
42:The reproduction panel is a native `details` element with the summary “Reproduce a game”. It contains the Board code input and Snapshot JSON textarea. Editing either field only edits a draft. `Load board` or `Load snapshot` performs the actual load. This separation lets a player inspect and correct copied text without replacing a running game on each keystroke.
44:`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.
46:The Board code control permits 32 characters and trims surrounding whitespace in `useGame.loadBoard`. The parser used inside JSON does not perform that trim. The Snapshot JSON control permits 65536 characters, while decoding separately enforces 65536 UTF-8 bytes. These are different measurements. A text field limit is an input affordance; the decoder remains the format boundary for programmatically supplied text too.
48:Successful load resets the board's remembered tab stop to its first position through a new session generation. Load and export buttons retain focus, with Resume handling its own disappearing-button focus transition. Focus is not serialized, so sharing a position cannot restore where the sender last tabbed. See [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) for interface details.
54:The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.
62:A board code also reveals enough information for a developer to regenerate the whole deck. That is its purpose. The browser still keeps hidden face identity out of hidden-card DOM content. Those facts are compatible: the shareable deterministic deal is a debugging tool, while the ordinary board presents the information available during play. [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md) describes validation and replacement behavior in more detail.
69:# Import safety policy
72:The important boundary is between a draft and accepted game data. A text field can contain arbitrary edits, and a replay file can contain arbitrary bytes decoded as text. Neither is treated as a `GameState` just because JSON parsing succeeds. Shape checks, numeric checks and game-specific consistency checks happen before the browser commits a replacement.
76:A field outside a format's declared shape is a validation failure, including inside a selection or replay action. The diagnostic policy makes that particular mistake identifiable to a person correcting copied data. An import with a field its format doesn't define shows "Unknown field: NAME." for the first such field and leaves the current state unchanged. This applies to the field diagnostic; it does not make an incomplete object or an unsupported version acceptable. The format's own required fields and state constraints still determine acceptance.
78:The implementation already rejects extra keys, but does not yet produce that field-specific notice. `hasExactKeys` returns a boolean, `decodeSnapshot` returns `null`, and the browser displays `Invalid snapshot.` for all snapshot failures. `readReplay` provides problem categories rather than the offending key name. The current adapters reject extensions without identifying the offending field as the diagnostic policy requires.
84:`useGame.loadSnapshot(text)` calls `decodeSnapshot(text)` first. A failed result calls the notice helper and returns `false`. Only a successful result reaches `clock.reset()` and `replaceGame(current.current, game, true)`. There is no earlier step that installs the imported code or clears the existing matched positions.
92:## The shared JSON boundary
94:The small helpers in `src/game/saved-format.ts` separate JSON mechanics from game validation:
99:| `parseJson(text)` | Returns parsed unknown data, or `undefined` after a parse exception |
100:| `isJsonObject(value)` | Accepts non-null objects except arrays |
104:`JSON.parse` can produce `null`, a list, a string, a boolean or a number. Those are valid JSON texts and invalid snapshot or replay roots. The object guard is what distinguishes them from a malformed text error. This is especially visible in replay results: `{` produces `malformedJson`, whereas `null` produces `format`.
106:`parseJson` does not execute input as code. A string containing script-like characters is still a string and fails where an object or number is required. The decoder does not merge the parsed object into the live session wholesale. It constructs the accepted state from a generated board and the fields it has validated.
110:The helpers operate on the parsed object, not the original token stream. JSON duplicate property names are consequently handled by `JSON.parse` before exact-key checking; the decoder does not retain a record of earlier overwritten occurrences. Likewise, numeric notation such as `1.0` becomes the number `1`. The integer predicate checks the value it receives rather than enforcing a preferred spelling of a JSON number.
114:Snapshot decoding measures its input before parsing and rejects text above `SNAPSHOT_MAX_BYTES`, which is `65_536`. Replay reading checks `REPLAY_MAX_BYTES`, which is `1_048_576`, before parsing. The replay parser then rejects more than `REPLAY_MAX_ACTIONS`, which is `10_000`. Trailing JSON whitespace is legal within the byte budget and still consumes that budget.
116:These checks bound the accepted format, but they should not be described as a streaming parser. `TextEncoder` allocates an encoded representation for measurement. The CLI also calls `readFile` before `readReplay` checks text size. A very large input can therefore already have been read into memory when it is rejected. The code provides explicit acceptance limits rather than a promise that arbitrary input has no allocation cost.
118:The browser textarea's `maxLength` is a separate character limit. Multibyte text can satisfy that limit and exceed the decoder's byte limit. The existing byte helper test uses an accented character to establish that bytes, rather than JavaScript string length, control acceptance. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) discusses how this interacts with readable export text.
122:After validating the version and board code, `decodeSnapshot` generates the board used to interpret positions. `readMatched` checks unique in-range positions and requires both copies of every represented face. An even-length list alone is not enough: on `np1-4-1`, `[2, 6]` is a pair while `[0, 1]` is not.
132:Evaluation can already have computed earlier actions when a later action fails. That is safe because the evolving state is local to `readReplay`; no browser session has been committed. The function returns a problem rather than that partial state. This is different from a streaming UI that visibly applies each imported action as it reads.
142:Replay reports have more detail. `readReplay` distinguishes file size, JSON syntax, root format, board code, actions array, end time, individual action shape, time order and index bounds. The CLI translates these into stderr text and uses a one-based action number for readers. Internal action positions remain zero-based. Mixing these conventions can lead an engineer to inspect the wrong action.
145:# Focus policy
147:This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.
149:Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.
153:`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.
155:A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.
157:The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.
161:The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.
163:The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.
165:A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.
169:New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.
171:The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.
173:A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.
175:Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.
177:## Remembered board focus
179:Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.
181:Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.
183:Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.
187:Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.
189:In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.
191:The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.
193:The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.
195:## Visible focus and scroll clearance
197:`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.
199:The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.
201:`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.
205:## Focus is not completion feedback
207:Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.
209:Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.
211:These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries.
215:The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring.
217:A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers these journeys with layout and input checks.
219:For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior.
228:The existing code already gives cards a minimum track size and shared controls a minimum height. Extending the interface calls for checking the actual rendered target in the phone layout, where flex wrapping and available width matter. Every new control is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels at a 390 pixel wide viewport. This policy covers the rendered control area rather than enlarging only a decorative child or a focus ring.
230:The current styles are useful building blocks, but they are not proof of every dimension for an arbitrary new element. In particular, `.control` declares minimum height without a general minimum width. A new short-label action could be tall enough while still being too narrow. The policy check and the existing class definition therefore answer related but different questions.
232:This is a control policy, not a claim of complete accessibility conformance. The visuals specification makes the same distinction for its chosen card minimum. Names, keyboard operation, contrast, visible focus and error behavior still have their own evidence. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers those areas without turning a size measurement into a blanket result.
238:| Card button | `board.css`, `card.css` | Grid tracks from 44px to 88px, square aspect ratio |
239:| Button, select, input, textarea using `.control` | `control.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 8px 12px |
240:| Reproduction summary | `reproduction.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 12px 16px |
256:A partially clipped card also has a full underlying button box. Clicking the visible part can activate it, after which the current implementation scrolls it fully into view. That behavior does not mean the clipping itself should be measured as the card's intended dimensions. It is an overflow case with a separate focus and pointer timing concern.
260:At `max-width: 599px`, the deal size group fills the row and uses space-between alignment. New Game and Restart receive `flex: 1`. This gives the actions room without hard-coding two button widths. The text and browser control still contribute their intrinsic size constraints.
264:A visual review at a wide desktop window can miss the consequences of a new wrapper or label. Selectors such as `.controls > button` and `.control-row > button` apply to direct children. If a wrapper changes which element grows, measuring the wrapper rather than the actual button can hide a target-width problem.
274:Focus outlines sit outside the control border and do not add activation area. Hover border changes likewise do not expand the target. Measurements used to assess the policy concern the actual element box; measurements used to assess focus visibility include outline width and offset. The project already has separate helpers for that distinction in `tests/focus-bounds.ts`.
280:The policy uses CSS pixels. Device pixel ratio affects the mapping to physical pixels, not the DOM geometry reported by `getBoundingClientRect`. A test at device scale 2 can still report a 44px CSS box. Multiplying the bounding-box result by device scale would answer a different question.
288:`tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks the default board and control dimensions at `320x640`. It measures `.controls button`, `.controls select` and `.card` boxes and checks minimum width and height. The same file checks large boards at phone and desktop viewports, where the card floor, viewport height and complete focus ring are important.
292:For a new feature review, a concise measurement record can identify the viewport, the control's role and name, its width and height and whether it is fully reachable. The record is most useful alongside the rendered layout, because it can reveal that a formally large button is covered by another element or forced beyond the page edge. This is observation of the target in context, not a second numerical policy.
294:The current game makes many of these checks straightforward by keeping interaction on native DOM elements. There is no canvas hit-map to reconcile with a drawn target. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains that architectural advantage, while [Contrast audit](../visuals/contrast-audit.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) cover other properties that a dimension alone cannot establish.

item.aggregated_output: ### docs/interface/dialog-policy.md # Dialog policy This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions. The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly. ## The confirmation boundary A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision. There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved. The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement. ## What the present controls actually do `Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used. BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation. The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure. This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle. ## Native behavior and application decisions The policy names a native element because the interface already relies on browser semantics for buttons, forms, selects and details. A dialog has a different interaction boundary from an ordinary panel. Its opening, cancellation and closing need to be considered as a coherent interaction rather than a div painted over the board. ### docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md # Text entry policy This page records the treatment of person-entered names and distinguishes it from the game's existing code and JSON fields. Neon Pairs currently asks for a board code and snapshot text, not a player name. There is no name field, group-name store or name rendering component in the source. The name policy below applies when such input is introduced; it does not describe a transformation already applied to the reproduction textarea. ## One name representation A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another. The policy is about a person's name. It does not turn all user input into name text, and it does not change the board-code grammar or snapshot serialization. The current fields demonstrate why that distinction matters: significant punctuation and structural whitespace belong to their own formats. This page explains representation and input boundaries without duplicating their conditions or error messages. ## Examples of representation The following examples use quotes only to make surrounding whitespace visible.
